The benchmark wars just changed shape. Artificial Analysis has released Intelligence Index v5 — its biggest methodology overhaul since January — and the headline isn't which model won. It's that the ground itself moved: 60% of the Index now runs on private test sets or held-out answers, making contamination — the quiet scandal of the LLM benchmark era — structurally much harder to pull off.

The scores: Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 58, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (max) at 57 and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 55. Anthropic and OpenAI hold the entire top five between them. Google's Gemini 4 Argon (high) sits next at 50. No single model sweeps the board — v5 splits the Index evenly across four domains at 25% each: Knowledge Work, Coding, Science, and General.

Three findings matter more than the ranking itself.

1. The open-weights gap just widened from 3 points to 12. Kimi K3.1 Pro tops the open-weights table at 46 — but its weights aren't released yet. Among models you can actually download and run, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) and GLM-5.3 (max) lead at 32 — a full 26 points behind the leader, and below even Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) at 36. If you're betting on open weights closing the frontier gap this year, this is the chart that says: not yet.

2. Cost per task varies by more than 13x among the leading models. Of the ten highest scorers, GPT-6.1 Terra (max) delivers an Intelligence Index task for $0.96, while Claude Fable 5.1 (max) costs $13.04 for the same unit of work. Same leaderboard, radically different economics. Procurement teams should read the price column before the score column.

3. The new benchmarks are agentic and practical. FrontierCode 2.0 — Cognition's private benchmark launched the same day — comprises 132 tasks in real open-source repositories, graded on whether a repository maintainer would actually merge the agent's change. Fail any blocking check and you score zero. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads it at 46%, with GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Terra and Claude Sonnet 5.5 all at 42%. The best open-weights performer, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, manages 28% — 18 points back. Terminal-Bench-Science adds 70 expert-curated scientific research tasks run in a live terminal, where every test must pass for credit.

There's also a new Progress Index v1, placing every model since November 2022 on one continuous capability scale — built, they note, on learnings from Epoch AI's Capabilities Index. It's the right split: Progress Index for capability over time, Intelligence Index for the current frontier.

The deeper story: evaluation is finally growing teeth. Public benchmarks saturate, leak into training data, and get gamed. Private held-out sets, merge-or-fail coding grades, and per-task cost accounting are what measurement looks like when a technology stops being a demo and becomes infrastructure. And the 23-point swing that reasoning effort alone can produce is a reminder that "which model is smartest" is increasingly the wrong question — the right one is "which model, at which effort level, at what cost, for which task."

The frontier is razor-thin at the top — one point between first and second. The gap that's widening is everywhere else.

Not sure how Indian AI companies (Like Sarvam) hosting Chinese open weights model companies ( Deepseek, Zhipu, Kimi) become "unpatriotic".. I am reading a lot of such foolish arguments being made.. 

Context - India's leading AI company, Sarvam recently announced that their infrastructure/GPUs will also host Chinese open weights models, besides Sarvam. Many on social media have been blasting Sarvam - saying that a company subsidized by the Indian govrnment to buy buy GPUs and infrastructure for model training, should NOT use these resources for "benefitting" Chinese models.

The entire argument is flawed, and quite foolish.

1. MONEY- When Chinese open weight models are run on Indian infrastructure- the revenue does NOT  go to Chinese companies. The revenue goes to the inference providers- which is Sarvam in this case. THis is the same reason that USA is NOT banning Chinese open weight companies, beucase they bring revenue to US inference companies like Fireworks AI, together, Base10, etc. 

2.  DATA.  When GPUs hosted in India run Chinese models, the data DOES NOT go to China. In fact all the data that previously would have gone to either US (GPT, Claude) or China (calling Deepseek, KImi via their APIs), will now STAY in India. 

3. DEMAND- Sarvam is NOT increasing demand for CHinese models. The demand already exisits. As per Open router, over 70% of global token volume is from Chinese Open weights models. Sarvam is just ernsuring that the revenue from this demand, as well as the DATA goes to India. 

UTILIZATION - Third-party model demand fills GPUs that would otherwise sit idle between Sarvam’s own workloads, lowering the cost per token for everything on the cluster. 

P.S - We arent investors in Sarvam - in fact we are investors in some of their biggest competitors, but let's given them credit where due.

https://t.co/kqiRXqGAHj MODEL RANKINGS: WHAT KIMI'S 354% SURGE REVEALS ABOUT THE CHANGING AI MARKET

The competitive landscape of Chinese AI models is becoming increasingly dynamic. https://t.co/kqiRXqGAHj's November 6–12 brand token ranking provides an interesting perspective on how developer demand is shifting across different model providers.

The most significant movement is not necessarily the model holding the top position, but the rapid changes happening beneath it.

Several figures deserve closer examination:

DeepSeek: Maintains the No. 1 position, demonstrating continued strength in model usage.
Qwen: Moves up three positions to No. 2, recording 5.31% weekly growth.
Kimi: Posts an impressive 354.11% week-over-week increase.
Tencent Hunyuan: Records 202.15% growth, indicating a substantial increase in activity.
MiniMax: Reaches a single-day peak within the overall Top 3.

THE IMPORTANT SIGNAL IS THE DISTRIBUTION OF DEMAND.

Kimi's growth is particularly striking, but percentage increases should be interpreted carefully. A large growth rate does not automatically translate into the largest market share or sustained leadership. Starting volume, absolute token consumption and consistency across multiple weeks all matter.

Qwen's rise is another interesting development. Moving three positions suggests improving competitive momentum, while DeepSeek's continued leadership indicates that established usage patterns remain difficult to displace.

Meanwhile, Hunyuan's growth following the addition of Hy4 to the API ecosystem raises an interesting possibility: new model releases and improved pricing can influence developer experimentation. However, the ranking alone cannot establish the cause of that increase.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR https://t.co/kqiRXqGAHj

A multi-model AI platform creates an environment where different providers compete for actual usage rather than relying exclusively on benchmark results or brand recognition.

For developers, this provides an opportunity to evaluate models through practical consumption patterns. For the platform, it offers insight into changing demand and the competitive position of different AI ecosystems.

My biggest takeaway is that AI competition is becoming increasingly fragmented. Leadership may remain stable at the top, but the middle of the ranking is becoming much more competitive.

The next important question is whether Kimi and Hunyuan can sustain their momentum or whether Qwen will consolidate its position at No. 2.

Everyone benchmarks coding agents on frontier $15/M-token cloud APIs. Almost nobody tests what happens when you put compiled AST rails underneath single-GPU open weights.

We ran 108 paired zero-hint brownfield episodes (temp=0.0 across Python, TypeScript, and Go) on six 8B-to-32B open-weight models sized for single 16GB-to-24GB cards:

• 14B-to-32B verified resolution jumped 3.1x: 27.8% stock (10/36) -> 86.1% with Nomos (31/36), cutting token spend by 43% to 57%.

• Hexagonal architecture boundary purity went from 0.0% across every unguarded model to 100% across Gemma 3 12B, Qwen 3 14B/32B, Mistral Small 24B, and local Qwen 3.8 27B (6/6 on a 16GB RTX 4080).

• Llama 3.1 8B hit a real capacity floor at 33.3% - proving rails amplify reasoning above ~12B rather than faking intelligence.

Are you routing everyday brownfield tickets to local 14B-32B workhorses yet, or still paying frontier rates for every edit?

The Strategic Advantage of a Unified Compute Settlement Layer

As AI models proliferate across specialized niches—reasoning, coding, video comprehension, and 4K multi-reference imaging—the complexity of managing compute supply grows exponentially.

A unified settlement layer positioned above every foundation model and beneath every autonomous agent solves the core infrastructure challenge of the multi-model era.

1. Abstraction Over Model Fragmentation

Your AI model might be open-source. But who controls the GPUs running it?

We talk a lot about open weights and model accessibility.

But if everyone relies on the same few infrastructure providers for inference, there's still a concentration problem. That's what makes @LightchainAI interesting to me.

Instead of depending on one large data center, the network allows independent operators to contribute GPU compute.

Workers can serve models such as Qwen, Llama, and gpt-oss from their own hardware.

The network routes inference jobs to participating workers and records which worker handled each response onchain.

Now Lightchain has also opened its Developer API on mainnet.

For developers already using an OpenAI-compatible chat API, the integration path is relatively familiar:
→ Change the base URL
→ Use the appropriate API key
→ Select a supported model

I like that approach because it focuses on making decentralized infrastructure usable, not just talking about decentralization.

Of course, the real test will be reliability, latency, pricing, and how well the worker network scales.

But giving developers another way to access open models is a direction worth watching.
